content.text: presentation thursday 4/30, 12 min + 3 Q&A, 3 speakers. outline slides please, and the 5 likeliest questions brooks asks

**Slides (12 min, ~10 slides)**

1. Title + team (Jordan, 0:20)
2. Why frustration in AI tutoring matters (Jordan, 1:00) — students ask the tutor before anyone else; nobody sees the struggle.
3. Definition: blocked goal + negative valence (David, 1:00)
4. Data: 412 transcripts, consent, de-identification (Jordan, 1:00)
5. Codebook: 7 codes in 2 groups (David, 1:30) — one example per group
6. Agreement: κ = 0.62, Fleiss 0.58; the REPEAT fix (David, 1:00)
7. Prevalence: 23.5% frustrated (David, 1:00)
8. **Struggle without expressed frustration: 14.8%** (David, 1:30) — the headline
9. Tutor features and frustration: regression (Maya, 2:00)
10. Design implications + limitations (Maya, 1:30)

**Likely questions**
1. *Why text-only? Isn't frustration multimodal?* — Because that's what the tutor sees; any intervention has to work from text.
2. *Is 0.58 Fleiss good enough?* — Moderate; it's on 30 sessions and we report it as a limitation; REPEAT fix came after.
3. *How do you know the "blocked-goal only" students are frustrated at all?* — We don't claim they are; we claim they're stuck without saying so, which is the point.
4. *Causality in the regression?* — None claimed; tutor responses and frustration influence each other.
5. *What would you build?* — A REPEAT detector that changes strategy (ask a question back, show a smaller step) instead of re-answering.
q3 is a good one. how do i answer it without sounding defensive

Lead with agreement, then the reframe:

> "Right, and we're careful not to call them frustrated. What we see is that they're blocked: they keep re-asking or drop off. They just don't say anything negative. That matters because a detector built on sentiment would miss all of them, and they're about one in seven sessions."

Short, concedes the point, and lands on why it's interesting.
